title: Choose COVAL’s dashboard direction
question: The instrument chart is assigned. Keep it, choose the fieldbook, explore another system, or re-roll.

options.label: Engineering Instrument Chart
options.lineage: Engineering calibration sheets and lab instrument panels
options.thesis: A calibrated field of people, projects, and work, where every mark helps an engineer locate the next useful connection.
options.viewport: A broad discovery surface pairs a measured project index with a narrow activity trace; people and recent work remain one turn away, while a visible demo label keeps seeded signals honest.
options.risk: Can feel clinical if the people behind the measurements recede.

raised.raise: People, projects, and recent work now read as one connected territory with clear transfer points between them.
Measurement states use line form and position as well as color, so differences remain legible without relying on hue alone.
A persistent destination rail keeps each workspace section reachable and its active section unmistakable.
A deliberate type scale separates names, project titles, and supporting details at every density.
Dense views keep a strict modular rhythm, with each row and column earning its place.
Every project or person entry can point directly to its related work, not a separate index to decipher.

regions.label: discovery index: projects and recent work

options.label: Engineer’s Fieldbook
options.lineage: Maintainer field notes and annotated engineering logbooks
options.thesis: A working fieldbook makes project records, contributor notes, and recent changes easy to scan and cross-reference.
options.viewport: The overview opens like a shared work log: recent project entries lead, names and contributors sit in the margins, and cross-references connect activity to its source.
options.risk: A familiar tool metaphor can feel ordinary unless the cross-references do real work.

options.label: Midnight Transit Diagram
options.thesis: Treat the team’s projects, people, and recent work as connected routes with useful transfer points.
options.viewport: An explorable team map puts project routes in the foreground, people at transfer stops, and recent work along each route.
options.case: Engineers recognize the wayfinding system and can follow relationships, but literal routes risk implying topology the demo data does not contain; it holds audience identification and loses product clarity.
options.risk: A literal subway geometry can imply a topology the product has not established.

options.label: Emission Line Rail
options.thesis: Read the dashboard as a series of signals, each tied back to its project and contributor.
options.viewport: A restrained signal rail previews recent work beside a searchable index of the projects and people generating each trace.
options.case: Engineers recognize the measurement language, but the rail makes recent work the main event and pushes people and projects into the background; it loses audience identification and product clarity.
options.kept: State can be carried by line height, dash, and doubling as well as color.
options.risk: Activity could overwhelm the people and projects engineers came to find.

options.label: Acetate Tab Manual
options.lineage: Technical reference manuals with layered acetate tabs
options.thesis: Turn each dashboard destination into a labeled section of a navigable reference manual.
options.viewport: A persistent tab rail opens directly into a project, people, activity, or message section.
options.case: Useful destination structure, but the documentation metaphor makes a living team feel static and harder to identify with.
options.kept: The tab system keeps cross-surface navigation visible and predictable.
options.risk: The manual frame can make exploration feel like lookup-only work.

options.label: Bitmap Specimen
options.lineage: Digital bitmap type specimens and early screen typography
options.thesis: Set team records in a pixel-built catalog with a clear typographic scale.
options.viewport: An indexed screen specimen puts member names, project labels, and recent work into a tightly ordered page.
options.case: Engineers may recognize the computer history, but the medium itself adds little clarity to the product’s relationships.
options.kept: The type scale remains explicit across dense and quiet views.
options.risk: Small pixel forms make long names and project metadata slower to scan.

options.label: Modular Grid Specimen
options.thesis: Fit the whole workspace to a consistent grid so every index and record feels composed.
options.viewport: Projects and people occupy a uniform grid, with recent work arranged in the same modular cells.
options.case: Dense alignment helps engineers compare records, but the grid alone does not help them discover relationships.
options.kept: A disciplined modular rhythm makes dense views easier to compare.
options.risk: Uniform cells flatten the difference between a person, a project, and an event.

options.label: Event Catalog Index
options.lineage: Independent publishing and convention hall catalogs
options.thesis: Let engineers browse a numbered catalog of people, projects, and activity with direct cross-references.
options.viewport: A compact listing acts as the main index, with a separate map connecting each listing to its team context.
options.case: Indexing maps cleanly to discovery, but the event catalog’s social setting is a poor fit for an engineering workspace.
options.kept: Direct cross-references make it easy to move from a listing to related work.
options.risk: The event frame makes a working team feel like a temporary exhibit.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A familiar admin dashboard with navigation, charts, and a grid of uniform summary cards.
canonCard.viewport: A standard analytics overview followed by a conventional sidebar and card grid.
canonCard.risk: Familiar structure makes it easy to scan but hides what is distinct about this workspace.
